Thursday, Beb. 2, 1933.
Dear et Leb-
We have been passing along the Aelutian Island all day. The islands run
from Alaska over to a point very near the Siberian coast. They are owned by the
United States and judging by what we saw of them today no other nation is very
likely to try to take them away from us. Great snow covered rocks rise out of
the Pacific apparently almost straight up, and from what t he various ship off-
icers say, entirely uninhabited.
They were beautiful in the sunshine of this
winter sky - some of the highest I would guess rising 1500 feet above the sea.
We ran within twenty or thirty miles of them.
Tonight we cross the 180th meridian, and so tomorrow will be Saturday,
instead of Friday. The weather has been very much better since Monday night,
and the crew all say that this has been to date a very smooth crossing for this
time of the year. It is very cold out and just now especially as the wind is
from the Northwest, blowing at a velosity of forty miles an hour, and coming
from across Siberta which as I guess you know is not a rival of Miami for the
Groeger and I had a Chinese dinner Monday night, chop sticks and all.
We started with "bird's nest" soup, then dried duck which was terrible,
a lot of side dishes which were suppose d to be great de licasies, followed
by a fish which was really quite good. It was worth the price of admission to
see Groeger worry with the Chinese steward about what every thing was before
he would eat it. All the time I knew that he would have given a lot for some
nice "pigs knuckles and kraut" but the poor fellow went the route like a good
sport. Today I asked him if he wanted another Chinese dinner tonight and he
just looked sort of pale and said he'd be willing to wait until we got to
where we might not be able to get anything else.
I played deck tennis today in the middle of a snow storm. It was the
exercise I have had on board, There are three or four Englishmen on
all destined for Oriental points to represent house s back "home" as
they call it,although some of them have spent most of their lives in China
Burma or elsewhere. They asked me to join them at deck tennis and it was a
lot of fun. Later we sat around a table in the taproo m and I had a lot of
fun listening to them talk of their experiences over a round of beers.
There are three couples on board, one of which is a Jew boy and his
bride. They have both been terribly sea sick all the time. They came up on deck
for a while today but about that time we ran out from behind the sheltering
coast of the Aelutians and the old ship began to roll and plung worse
ever, so they beat a hasty retreat and I guess we wont see them again for a
while. The other couples are older and appear to be on a cruise - all most

Now all
the stewards from
nearby empty tables gather around in respectful amusement to see who among
them can make out what I am trying to
convey.
Think I will give it up
though because there are so many dialects that even if you are good, no
one except a man from the same district as your instruoter could understand.
stop now to dress for dinner. Another shot tomorrow for small pox
and the final shot for typhoid on Tuesday. Will write again and hope there
will be more to write about. There
is nothing at all doing on board. We all
turn in about ten oclock.
After dinner if there isn't a movie we sit around
and read or work on jig saw puzzles of which there are several devilish one
in the taproom - nearly went blind working one out last night.
